name: Maxillary distraction osteogenesis

lead: In maxillary distraction, the upper jaw is cut and then slowly pulled forward by a device so new bone forms in the gap. It is used mainly for severe upper-jaw underdevelopment such as in cleft lip and palate.
Studies compare it with conventional advancement for relapse and stability; a Cochrane review found too little evidence for general conclusions.

paras: After a cut, a latency of about a week, and activation at roughly 1 mm per day, a consolidation period lets the new bone mature before the device is removed.

Reported complications include infection, unintended direction of bone growth, hardware failure and, in craniofacial distraction generally, nerve injury. External devices carry pin-site infection and scarring risks.

lead: Maxillary distraction osteogenesis (MDO) is a surgical technique for advancing the upper jaw gradually. The bone is cut, a distraction device is attached, and the segments are slowly separated so new bone forms in the gap, rather than moving the jaw in one step as in conventional orthognathic surgery.[1][2]

Its main published use is severe maxillary hypoplasia, especially in cleft lip and palate. Early reports from the late 1990s described rigid external devices used in children and adolescents with severe deficiency.[3][4][5][6] It has also been used in combination with mandibular distraction in hemifacial microsomia.[7]

Studies have compared it with orthognathic surgery in cleft patients for morbidity, relapse and five-year stability.[8][9] A 2018 Cochrane review, as summarized by Wikipedia, found only one small study (47 participants) on maxillary distraction in cleft lip and palate, insufficient for general conclusions.[1] In looksmaxxing contexts it is mentioned as a more extensive alternative to Le Fort I advancement.
infobox: Severe maxillary hypoplasia, e.g. cleft lip and palate

paras: Distraction osteogenesis proceeds in phases: an osteotomy and device placement, a latency period of about seven days, an activation phase in which the segments are separated by roughly 1 mm per day, and a consolidation phase while new bone matures, after which the device is removed in a second operation.[1] One description of maxillary use reports advancements of about 8-15 mm and stable bite and speech improvement in cleft patients, with vector control considered essential.[2]

Devices may be external, such as the rigid external frames described in the 1990s cleft literature,[3][4] or internal. External devices allow monitoring and adjustment but carry pin-site infection and scarring risk, according to one summary.[2]

Reports describe maxillary distraction in children in mixed dentition with cleft lip and palate and in prognathic patients, aiming at aesthetic and functional benefit.[5] Another series analyzed cephalometric results in 14 cleft patients.[6] Studies have examined changes in speech[10] and in the soft-tissue profile at one year[11] after distraction. A pilot study combined adeno-tonsillectomy with rapid maxillary distraction in pre-pubertal children.[12]

A 2006 study compared cleft maxillary distraction with orthognathic surgery on morbidity and relapse,[8] and a 2010 study followed stability over five years.[9] A 2013 systematic review, cited by Wikipedia, found low-quality evidence comparing the two, with both approaches potentially effective and distraction possibly reducing long-term relapse.[13]

Across craniofacial distraction generally, complications reported include infection (about 5% overall), unintended bone growth direction (7-9%), hardware failure (3-4.5%) and protocol deviations.[1] Pin-site infection in a wide range of sites and device failure are also described.[2] Relapse and the need for later orthognathic surgery are discussed in cleft studies.[8][9]

Published human studies are mostly case series and comparative cohorts in cleft and hypoplasia patients.[3][4][5][6][8][9] Registered trials include a phase 2 comparison of cleft orthognathic surgery and distraction (n=60),[14] a study of rigid fixation after device removal and relapse (n=20),[15] and an observational comparison of tooth-borne, bone-borne and hybrid distraction after surgically assisted expansion (n=90).[16] No studies of cosmetic use in people without a deformity were found.
